title_eng: Feasibility Study for Unconstrained Respiration Monitoring Based on Multi-Way Approach Using an Acceleration and Force Sensing Module
abstract:
3482 IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 17, NO. 11, JUNE 1, 2017
Feasibility Study for Unconstrained Respiration
Monitoring Based on Multi-Way Approach Using
an Acceleration and Force Sensing Module
Sooji Park and Hangsik Shin, Member, IEEE
Abstract— The purpose of this paper was to validate the
feasibility of a proposed sensing module for multiway respira-
tory monitoring. The proposed monitoring system was imple-
mented using an ultralow-power microcontroller, that included a
three-axis accelerometer, an analog/digital input port to connect
to an external sensor, and a Bluetooth module for wireless com-
munication. We developed an accelerometer-equipped wireless
sensing module and a layered-architecture external strip-type
force sensor interface for respiration monitoring. In the feasibility
experiment, the accelerometer-equipped module was inserted in
a pillow and strip-type force sensors were placed under each
of the head, chest, and abdomen to investigate the performance
of the respiration measurement in terms of the measurement
position. Twelve subjects participated in the experiment, and
signals from the accelerometer and the strip-type force sensor
were simultaneously recorded during sleep. The results of the
experiment showed that the devia tion in length of the respiration
cycle was estimated with error s under 250 ms in the acceleration
signal and the signal from the strip force sensors.
Index Terms— Accelerometer, strip force sensing resistor, res-
piration monitoring, sleep monitoring, unconstrained monitoring.

stable environments is necessary for physiological monitoring.
However, it is difﬁcult to meet such a requirement in mobile
and everyday environments. Therefore, unconstrained monitor-
ing technology has attracted research interest as another type
of u-health technology for long-term monitoring.
In particular, physiological monitoring during sleep provides
the advantage of stable data recording over a long stretch of
time. Moreover, managing sleep disorders such as sleep apnea
and snoring is of fundamental importance for health since
these disorders can negatively impact sleep quality and body
balance, leading to difﬁculties in concentration, fatigue, and
cognition [1]–[3]. Finally, sleep disorders not only negatively
affect daily activities, but also cause cardiovascular disease and
can lead to sudden death during sleep in serious cases [4], [5].
Polysomnography (PSG) is a traditional method for sleep
analysis [6], but there is a need for methods that are more
convenient because PSG is expensive and requires compli-
cated preparation. In an atte mpt to simplify PSG, wearable
monitoring devices, such as head bands or wrist bands, have
been introduced [7]. However, such devices constrain user’s
behavior during sleep, cause discomfort, and ultimately inter-
fere with sleep. These methods can sometimes be used to
diagnose disease, but they are difﬁcult to use all the time
in everyday life. As such, unconstrained monitoring has the
advantage of being able to acquire steady and continuous bio-
signals. Although most unconstrained measurement techniques
are vulnerable to motion noise, sleeping is an activity that
generates the smallest motion artifacts during the day, thus an
unconstrained technique is suitable for use in daily monitoring.
Numerous unconstrained sleep-monitoring methods have
been proposed, and actimetry is a representative method that
records acceleration signals and is essential to monitor ambula-
tory activity and as well as sleep [8]. Other methods that were
proposed to be comfortable for sleep monitoring use pressure-
sensitive textiles [9], [10], piezoelectric ﬁlms [11], [12],
ultrasound [13], ultra-wide band (UWB) radar [14], opti-
cal ﬁbers [15], or wireless signals [16]. Smartphone-based
sleep tracking technologies have also been commercial-
ized [8], [17], [18]. In the view of the technological improve-
ments and diverse uses, more effective and ﬂexible devices for
sleep monitoring are expected to be introduced in the future.
Unconstrained monitoring senses the user’s respira-
tion or heart rate using bed-based, mattress-based, or some
other kind of sensing platform [12], [19]–[21]. These pressure-
based sensing devices can provide sleep-related information,
including respiration rate and heart rate, by making direct

contact with the human body. However, portability is one
of the most signiﬁcant limitations of mattress or ﬁlm-type
monitoring devices. Moreover, the cost of such systems is
relatively high because the sen sing area needs to be wide and
raw materials, such as polyvinylidene diﬂuoride (PVDF) or an
air mattress, are expensive. Strip-type sleep monitoring devices
were recently proposed, and these use a piezoelectric sen-
sor [22], which makes them easier to use and less expensive
than PVDF [11], [12] or air mattress [23] sensors. Moreover,
a narrow width sensor is less susceptible to motion noise than a
wide-area sensor since unnece ssary contact can be minimized.
With this in mind, we propose an unconstrained sleep
monitoring device that uses an accelerometer or a strip-type
force sensor suitable for diverse user needs. The proposed
sensing platform can operate as a standalone device without
any additional sensors due to the presence of an accelerometer.
Moreover, it could provide plen tiful, accurate information
when using additional external sensors, such as a strip-type
force sensor. In this study, we implemented the proposed
system and experimentally tested its feasibility.
II. M ATERIALS AND METHODS
A. System Overview
he proposed sensing system has a simple structure and
consists of a microcontroller unit (MCU), 3-axis accelerome-
ter, wireless communication module, rechargeable battery, and
analog/digital input ports. The system is designed to support
two different operational modes: standalone mode and station
mode. In the standalone mode, the system uses an embed-
ded accelerometer to record 3- axis acceleration without the
need for external sensors. The standalone mode is extremely
simple to use without any additional devices, so it is useful
in various situations requiring convenient monitoring. In the
station mode, the sensing system can record multiple signals
using internal and external sensors simultaneously. In this
study, the signal from the internal accelerometer and a force
signal from an external sensor are recorded. In this mode,
the proposed system operates as a base station to record and
transfer the signals. The station mode has more uses and
provides sophisticated results with data from various external
sensors. However, this mode requires additional sensors and
more space for installation. Fig. 1 shows the overall concept
for the proposed system.
B. System Implementation
The proposed system is implemented using the ultra-
low-power MSP430G2553 microprocessor (Texas Instruments
Inc., TX, USA), which includes a 10-bit analog-to-digital
converter. In the standby mode, it has a clock speed of up
to 16 MHz and power consumption of about 0.7 µA [24].
In low power mode 4 (LPM4) operation, MSP430 turns off
the CPU as well as all clocks. Thus, the power consumption
can be minimized ( ∼0.1 µA), and the operation time of a
continuous monitoring device can be prolonged. Therefore,
the proposed system can provide reasonable performance when
continuous long-term monitoring is required. The system is
capable of both wired and wirel ess communication (serial
communication using RS232 and Bluetooth, respectively) to
transfer the measured data. Fig. 2 shows a schematic of the
proposed system (Fig. 2(a)), the schematic of the external
strip-type force sensor interface (Fig. 2(b)), a prototype of
the implemented sensing module and the external strip-type
force sensor interface (Fig. 2(c)), and the external strip-type
force sensor and sensor connection (Fig. 2(d)). We employed
the ADXL335 3-axis acceleromet er (Analog Devices Inc.,
MA, USA), which is small, consumes a low amount of power,
and offers a typical dynamic range of ±3.6g with average
sensitivity of 300 mV/g (@V s = 3 V). Its bandwidth is
1,600 Hz on the x-a n d y-axes and 550 Hz on the z-axis [25].
C. Strip-Type Force Sensor
The proposed strip-type force sensor is a ﬂexible sensor
with a narrow band shape and piezo-resistive characteristic in
which the resistance value changes depending on the applied
force. Respiration is measured by sensing the force or pressure
between the human body and the mattress according to the
change in volume of the chest cavity during respiration.
Among various force or pressure sensors, load cell type
sensors are too rigid and thick and thus are not human-friendly.
In addition, since conventional force/pressure sensors have a
speciﬁc shape and size – with a rectangular or circular shape
of several centimeters – the measurement accuracy depends
critically on the measurement site. The strip type sensor
that was used in this study is a ﬂexible, thin, long strip.
Therefore, the strip type sensor has few restrictions in terms
of the measurement position and can help record a signal with
greater accuracy since it can be easily placed on the bed.
The strip-type force sensor used in the present study con-
sists of a commercially-available force-sensing resistor (FSR),
FSR-408 (Interlink Electronics, MA, USA) [26] with a
polyester-based textile cover. FSR-408 is a single-zone FSR
optimized for use in human touch control applications and
electronic devices, such as medical systems. An FSR is a two-
wire device with a robust polymer thick ﬁlm (PTF) sensor
that exhibits a decrease in resistance with an increase in force
applied to the sensor surface. It is available in any active
length, up to an active area of 609.6 mm × 10.2 mm (width)
